Nuestro nombre fusiona la potencia y versatilidad del microcontrolador ESP32 con la inmensidad y el horizonte sin límites del espacio, representando nuestra capacidad de escalar soluciones inteligentes desde una placa de desarrollo hasta los retos más ambiciosos de la exploración actual.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink Viewer is a public web tool that lets anyone see how a region of the sky changes over time in images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Users enter right ascension and declination, or pick a preset target, and get a blink-style image sequence that helps spot objects that move or change in brightness.

A FastAPI server queries the IRSA archive with astroquery, downloads the spectral images covering that position, and converts them into easy-to-view frames. It also caches results so later requests load almost instantly. The viewer, available in English and Spanish, lets users adjust playback speed, zoom, contrast, and pixel inversion.

It matters because SPHEREx data is public but stored in FITS files that are hard to use without programming. Our tool lowers that barrier for students, teachers, and amateur astronomers, and makes new astronomical data easier to explore.
details:
What it does and how it works

SPHEREx Blink Viewer is a public web tool where users enter right ascension and declination, or pick a preset target, and get a blink-style image sequence of that sky region. This makes it easy to spot objects that move or change in brightness. A FastAPI server queries NASA’s IRSA archive with astroquery and downloads the SPHEREx spectral images covering that position. It then converts them, using astropy and numpy, into frames that are easy to view in the browser. Results are cached, so repeated requests load almost instantly.

Benefits

SPHEREx data is public, but it is stored in FITS files that are hard to open without programming. Our tool removes that barrier: nothing to install, no code to write, no gigabytes to download. It works in English and Spanish, and users can adjust playback speed, zoom, contrast, and image inversion.

Expected impact

We want students, teachers, amateur astronomers, and scientists from other fields to explore new astronomical data with nothing but curiosity. It can serve as a classroom resource, support citizen science, and act as a first look before deeper analysis.

Tools used

Python, FastAPI, astroquery (IRSA access), astropy and numpy (FITS reading and processing), HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the viewer, and server-side caching to speed up requests.

Creativity

We changed the question from “how do I download this data?” to “how do I look at it?”. We took blinking, a classic technique for finding moving objects, and made it available in any browser. Technical files become something close to a video of the sky.

Factors we considered

We prioritized accessibility (no installation, bilingual) and speed (cropped regions, caching, parallel downloads). We also made sure the viewer shows only what it truly computes. IRSA is an external service that can be unstable, so caching and a recorded demo serve as backups.
